voiceover.text: Last time, one trend line stood out: insufficient sleep on school nights. First, pick the youth health issue you'd most want changed, and write one sentence saying what you'd do about it. Keep that sentence. We'll test it at the end.

The syllabus gives you seven questions for one issue, in order. The first is its nature, and people rush it. Mental health isn't an issue you can research, it's a field. Psychological distress among fifteen to nineteen year olds is an issue: it names a condition, a population and an age range, and it's actually measured. Describe it in four parts: what it is, who it affects, over what period, and how it's measured. Ours is insufficient sleep among fifteen to seventeen year olds on school nights.

Second, what does the data tell us? Ask the five questions you use for any table, plus two more. Is it split by group, since an average hides the gap? And what does the measure miss? Here's real data. In twenty twenty-three, the ABS measured sleep with a wrist sensor. Twelve to seventeen year olds averaged seven hours fifty-six minutes a night, against a guideline of eight to ten hours from age fourteen. Those with screens in the bedroom slept twenty-nine minutes less. But the age band starts at twelve, and school nights aren't reported separately. So quote the source and year, and say what the data can't see.

Third, why is this an issue? Saying it's bad earns nothing. Argue on three grounds, and use at least two. Burden: sleep loss affects mood, concentration, learning, injury risk and immune function, so it feeds several other issues at once. Equity: it falls harder where homes are crowded or noisy, or a student works late shifts. Leverage: in adolescence the body clock shifts later, so sleepiness arrives later, but the school alarm doesn't move.

Fourth, protective factors. For sleep: a consistent routine, a dark, quiet room, screens out of the bedroom, a later school start, and limits on late paid shifts. Mark each one: can the young person build it, or must someone else provide it? Only the routine, and partly the screens, sit with the young person. The rest are conditions.

Fifth, what's already being done? Check this first, because what happened before is the evidence. Strategies work at five levels. Regulation changes what's allowed or what it costs. Services change what help you can reach. Education changes what people know. Environment changes what's easy. Community and peer strategies change who's trusted. For sleep, nearly everything sits on one level: education, sleep hygiene advice. Some schools overseas have moved to later starts, which is environment.

Now evaluate, with three questions. Who does it reach? Advice is easiest to follow if you already have a quiet room and a free evening, so it can lift the average and widen the gap. Which level does it work on? Changing conditions tends to beat changing knowledge. And how would anyone know it worked? Without a measure decided in advance, a strategy can be defended, but not evaluated. Look at smoking. It fell among young Australians through advertising limits, tax, plain packaging, smoke-free places and education, together over decades. Combinations across levels beat single strategies.

scenes.title: five tests for a new strategy

voiceover.text: Sixth, propose a new strategy that follows from your analysis, and run five tests. Does it address a cause you found, or only a symptom? Does it work at an empty level? Who will it reach, and who will it miss? Does it meet the social justice principles, especially participation? And how will you evaluate it: a measure, a timeframe, and a result that would make you drop it? Three of these you've just used. Keep this checklist; it'll grow.

For sleep, the empty levels are environment and regulation. So, a later start for senior years, from nine thirty, plus a policy, agreed with local employers, that seniors aren't rostered past nine pm on school nights. Design it with a student advisory group. It helps least those in crowded or noisy homes, so add a quiet study space at school. Then measure school-night sleep before and twelve months after, for the students sleeping least. If they don't improve, it's failed, whatever the average does.

scenes.title: the seventh question, and the shape

voiceover.text: Seventh, what do you still need to know? Does a later start lengthen sleep, or do bedtimes just shift later? Studies overseas suggest sleep gets longer, but would that hold here, for the students sleeping least? That open question is where research becomes advocacy, arguing for change on behalf of a group. And notice the shape. If you could delete your first five answers and your proposal wouldn't change, it didn't come from the research.
Two things to remember. Seven questions, in order, and the order is the method. And a strategy that can't fail can't be evaluated.

Two exam questions. First. A school group writes, "Our campaign will raise awareness of youth mental health. Success will be measured by how many posters we distribute." Identify the test that its measure of success fails, explain why, and repair it. Pause here to answer.

It fails the evaluation test. It also names no cause, but its clearest failure is the measure. Counting posters measures the campaign's activity, not any change in health. A repair names an outcome in advance, like help-seeking contacts at the school service, before and after, and a result that would count as failure. The classic mistake is counting what you did, not what changed.
Second. Propose a new strategy to address one health issue for young people, and justify why it would be effective. Pause here to answer.

Lead with the cause you found, then the empty level, so it isn't one more campaign. Make the strategy concrete, ideally at two levels, designed with young people. Name who it will miss and what you'd add. Finish with a measure that could show it failed. The classic mistake is a good idea with no cause behind it.

Now run your sentence from the start through the five tests. Pause the video if you want to try it. Next, we'll open the protective factors row, and the personal skills that protect a young person's health.
